stem: The vapour pressure of pure liquids A and B are \(450\) and \(700\,\text{mm Hg}\) respectively, at \(350\,\text{K}\). Find out the composition of the liquid mixture if total vapour pressure is \(600\,\text{mm Hg}\). Also find the composition of the vapour phase.

subtopic: Colligative Properties and Determination of Molar Mass
stem: The vapour pressure of pure benzene at a certain temperature is \(0.850\,\text{bar}\). A non-volatile, non-electrolyte solid weighing \(0.5\,\text{g}\) when added to \(39.0\,\text{g}\) of benzene (molar mass \(78\,\text{g mol}^{-1}\)). Vapour pressure of the solution, then, is \(0.845\,\text{bar}\). What is the molar mass of the solid substance?
solution:
The various quantities known to us are as follows:

\(p_1^{0} = 0.850\,\text{bar}\); \(p = 0.845\,\text{bar}\); \(M_1 = 78\,\text{g mol}^{-1}\); \(w_2 = 0.5\,\text{g}\); \(w_1 = 39\,\text{g}\)

Substituting these values in equation (2.28), we get

\(\dfrac{0.850\,\text{bar} - 0.845\,\text{bar}}{0.850\,\text{bar}} = \dfrac{0.5\,\text{g} \times 78\,\text{g mol}^{-1}}{M_2 \times 39\,\text{g}}\)

Therefore, \(M_2 = 170\,\text{g mol}^{-1}\)
_note: The book's printed solution cites "equation (2.28)"; the equation it substitutes into is (1.28) on the preceding page. Stale cross-reference from an earlier edition in which this was Chapter 2. Transcribed as printed.

subtopic: Colligative Properties and Determination of Molar Mass
stem: \(18\,\text{g}\) of glucose, \(\text{C}_6\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_6\), is dissolved in \(1\,\text{kg}\) of water in a saucepan. At what temperature will water boil at \(1.013\,\text{bar}\)? \(K_b\) for water is \(0.52\,\text{K kg mol}^{-1}\).
solution:
Moles of glucose \(= 18\,\text{g} / 180\,\text{g mol}^{-1} = 0.1\,\text{mol}\)

Number of kilograms of solvent \(= 1\,\text{kg}\)

Thus molality of glucose solution \(= 0.1\,\text{mol kg}^{-1}\)

For water, change in boiling point

\(\Delta T_b = K_b \times m = 0.52\,\text{K kg mol}^{-1} \times 0.1\,\text{mol kg}^{-1} = 0.052\,\text{K}\)

Since water boils at \(373.15\,\text{K}\) at \(1.013\,\text{bar}\) pressure, therefore, the boiling point of solution will be \(373.15 + 0.052 = 373.202\,\text{K}\).

subtopic: Colligative Properties and Determination of Molar Mass
stem: The boiling point of benzene is \(353.23\,\text{K}\). When \(1.80\,\text{g}\) of a non-volatile solute was dissolved in \(90\,\text{g}\) of benzene, the boiling point is raised to \(354.11\,\text{K}\). Calculate the molar mass of the solute. \(K_b\) for benzene is \(2.53\,\text{K kg mol}^{-1}\).
solution:
The elevation \((\Delta T_b)\) in the boiling point \(= 354.11\,\text{K} - 353.23\,\text{K} = 0.88\,\text{K}\)

Substituting these values in expression (2.33) we get

\(M_2 = \dfrac{2.53\,\text{K kg mol}^{-1} \times 1.8\,\text{g} \times 1000\,\text{g kg}^{-1}}{0.88\,\text{K} \times 90\,\text{g}} = 58\,\text{g mol}^{-1}\)

Therefore, molar mass of the solute, \(M_2 = 58\,\text{g mol}^{-1}\)
_note: The book's printed solution cites "expression (2.33)"; the equation used is (1.33) on the preceding page — the same stale Chapter-2 cross-reference as Eg 1.6. The page also prints the subtraction as "353. 23 K" with a stray space after the decimal point; transcribed as 353.23 K.

subtopic: Colligative Properties and Determination of Molar Mass
stem: \(45\,\text{g}\) of ethylene glycol \((\text{C}_2\text{H}_6\text{O}_2)\) is mixed with \(600\,\text{g}\) of water. Calculate (a) the freezing point depression and (b) the freezing point of the solution.
solution:
Depression in freezing point is related to the molality, therefore, the molality of the solution with respect to ethylene glycol \(= \dfrac{\text{moles of ethylene glycol}}{\text{mass of water in kilogram}}\)

Moles of ethylene glycol \(= \dfrac{45\,\text{g}}{62\,\text{g mol}^{-1}} = 0.73\,\text{mol}\)

Mass of water in kg \(= \dfrac{600\,\text{g}}{1000\,\text{g kg}^{-1}} = 0.6\,\text{kg}\)

Hence molality of ethylene glycol \(= \dfrac{0.73\,\text{mol}}{0.60\,\text{kg}} = 1.2\,\text{mol kg}^{-1}\)

Therefore freezing point depression,

\(\Delta T_f = 1.86\,\text{K kg mol}^{-1} \times 1.2\,\text{mol kg}^{-1} = 2.2\,\text{K}\)

Freezing point of the aqueous solution \(= 273.15\,\text{K} - 2.2\,\text{K} = 270.95\,\text{K}\)
_note: Font-substitution artifact on the printed page: the delta in the freezing-point-depression line is set as a Latin "Ä" (it reads "ÄT_f = 1.86 K kg mol^-1 ..."). Every other occurrence in the chapter is a proper Δ, so this is a typesetting fault, not a different symbol; transcribed as \Delta T_f.

subtopic: Colligative Properties and Determination of Molar Mass
stem: \(1.00\,\text{g}\) of a non-electrolyte solute dissolved in \(50\,\text{g}\) of benzene lowered the freezing point of benzene by \(0.40\,\text{K}\). The freezing point depression constant of benzene is \(5.12\,\text{K kg mol}^{-1}\). Find the molar mass of the solute.
solution:
Substituting the values of various terms involved in equation (1.36) we get,

\(M_2 = \dfrac{5.12\,\text{K kg mol}^{-1} \times 1.00\,\text{g} \times 1000\,\text{g kg}^{-1}}{0.40 \times 50\,\text{g}} = 256\,\text{g mol}^{-1}\)

Thus, molar mass of the solute \(= 256\,\text{g mol}^{-1}\)
_note: The printed denominator is "0.40 × 50 g" — the unit K is dropped from the 0.40 (it is ΔT_f = 0.40 K). Transcribed as printed; the numerical result 256 g mol^-1 is unaffected.

subtopic: Colligative Properties and Determination of Molar Mass
stem: \(200\,\text{cm}^3\) of an aqueous solution of a protein contains \(1.26\,\text{g}\) of the protein. The osmotic pressure of such a solution at \(300\,\text{K}\) is found to be \(2.57 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{bar}\). Calculate the molar mass of the protein.
solution:
The various quantities known to us are as follows: \(\Pi = 2.57 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{bar}\),

\(V = 200\,\text{cm}^3 = 0.200\,\text{litre}\)

\(T = 300\,\text{K}\)

\(R = 0.083\,\text{L bar mol}^{-1}\,\text{K}^{-1}\)

Substituting these values in equation (2.42) we get

\(M_2 = \dfrac{1.26\,\text{g} \times 0.083\,\text{L bar K}^{-1}\,\text{mol}^{-1} \times 300\,\text{K}}{2.57 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{bar} \times 0.200\,\text{L}} = 61{,}022\,\text{g mol}^{-1}\)
_note: The book's printed solution cites "equation (2.42)"; the equation used is (1.42) on the preceding page — the third instance in this band of the stale Chapter-2 cross-reference (see also Eg 1.6 and Eg 1.8).

subtopic: Colligative Properties and Determination of Molar Mass
stem: Calculate the osmotic pressure in pascals exerted by a solution prepared by dissolving \(1.0\,\text{g}\) of polymer of molar mass \(185{,}000\) in \(450\,\text{mL}\) of water at \(37\,^\circ\text{C}\).

\(2\,\text{g}\) of benzoic acid \((\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COOH})\) dissolved in \(25\,\text{g}\) of benzene shows a depression in freezing point equal to \(1.62\,\text{K}\). Molal depression constant for benzene is \(4.9\,\text{K kg mol}^{-1}\). What is the percentage association of acid if it forms dimer in solution?
solution:
The given quantities are: \(w_2 = 2\,\text{g}\); \(K_f = 4.9\,\text{K kg mol}^{-1}\); \(w_1 = 25\,\text{g}\), \(\Delta T_f = 1.62\,\text{K}\)

Substituting these values in equation (1.36) we get:

\(M_2 = \dfrac{4.9\,\text{K kg mol}^{-1} \times 2\,\text{g} \times 1000\,\text{g kg}^{-1}}{25\,\text{g} \times 1.62\,\text{K}} = 241.98\,\text{g mol}^{-1}\)

Thus, experimental molar mass of benzoic acid in benzene is \(= 241.98\,\text{g mol}^{-1}\)

Now consider the following equilibrium for the acid:

\(2\,\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COOH} \rightleftharpoons (\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COOH})_2\)

If \(x\) represents the degree of association of the solute then we would have \((1 - x)\) mol of benzoic acid left in unassociated form and correspondingly \(\dfrac{x}{2}\) as associated moles of benzoic acid at equilibrium. Therefore, total number of moles of particles at equilibrium is:

\(1 - x + \dfrac{x}{2} = 1 - \dfrac{x}{2}\)

Thus, total number of moles of particles at equilibrium equals van't Hoff factor \(i\).

But \(i = \dfrac{\text{Normal molar mass}}{\text{Abnormal molar mass}} = \dfrac{122\,\text{g mol}^{-1}}{241.98\,\text{g mol}^{-1}}\)

or \(\dfrac{x}{2} = 1 - \dfrac{122}{241.98} = 1 - 0.504 = 0.496\)

or \(x = 2 \times 0.496 = 0.992\)

Therefore, degree of association of benzoic acid in benzene is \(99.2\,\%\).

stem: \(0.6\,\text{mL}\) of acetic acid \((\text{CH}_3\text{COOH})\), having density \(1.06\,\text{g mL}^{-1}\), is dissolved in \(1\,\text{litre}\) of water. The depression in freezing point observed for this strength of acid was \(0.0205\,^\circ\text{C}\). Calculate the van't Hoff factor and the dissociation constant of acid.
solution:
Number of moles of acetic acid \(= \dfrac{0.6\,\text{mL} \times 1.06\,\text{g mL}^{-1}}{60\,\text{g mol}^{-1}} = 0.0106\,\text{mol} = n\)

Molality \(= \dfrac{0.0106\,\text{mol}}{1000\,\text{mL} \times 1\,\text{g mL}^{-1}} = 0.0106\,\text{mol kg}^{-1}\)

Using equation (1.35)

\(\Delta T_f = 1.86\,\text{K kg mol}^{-1} \times 0.0106\,\text{mol kg}^{-1} = 0.0197\,\text{K}\)

van't Hoff Factor \((i) = \dfrac{\text{Observed freezing point}}{\text{Calculated freezing point}} = \dfrac{0.0205\,\text{K}}{0.0197\,\text{K}} = 1.041\)

Acetic acid is a weak electrolyte and will dissociate into two ions: acetate and hydrogen ions per molecule of acetic acid. If \(x\) is the degree of dissociation of acetic acid, then we would have \(n(1 - x)\) moles of undissociated acetic acid, \(nx\) moles of \(\text{CH}_3\text{COO}^-\) and \(nx\) moles of \(\text{H}^+\) ions,

\(\text{CH}_3\text{COOH} \rightleftharpoons \text{H}^+ + \text{CH}_3\text{COO}^-\)

\(n\) mol, \(0\), \(0\)

\(n(1 - x)\), \(nx\) mol, \(nx\) mol

Thus total moles of particles are: \(n(1 - x + x + x) = n(1 + x)\)

\(i = \dfrac{n(1 + x)}{n} = 1 + x = 1.041\)

Thus degree of dissociation of acetic acid \(= x = 1.041 - 1.000 = 0.041\)

Then \([\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}] = n(1 - x) = 0.0106\,(1 - 0.041)\),

\([\text{CH}_3\text{COO}^-] = nx = 0.0106 \times 0.041\), \([\text{H}^+] = nx = 0.0106 \times 0.041\).

\(K_a = \dfrac{[\text{CH}_3\text{COO}^-][\text{H}^+]}{[\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}]} = \dfrac{0.0106 \times 0.041 \times 0.0106 \times 0.041}{0.0106\,(1.00 - 0.041)} = 1.86 \times 10^{-5}\)
_note: The observed depression is stated as 0.0205 °C in the stem and then used as 0.0205 K in the van't Hoff ratio; the two are equal as a temperature DIFFERENCE, so the arithmetic is sound. Transcribed as printed.
